title: Ashland reports third quarter 2026 results and reaffirms full-year sales & Adjusted EBITDA outlook
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Ashland Inc.'s business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: PDF Version Sales of $497 million, up seven percent from the prior-year quarter Income from continuing operations of $41 million, or $0.89 per diluted share Adjusted Income from Continuing Operations Excluding Intangibles Amortization Expense of $47 million, or $1.02 per diluted share Net income of $16 million, or $0.35 per diluted share Sales volumes rose six percent from the prior-year quarter, with gains achieved across all business units Adjusted EBITDA of $109 million, down four percent from the prior-year quarter, primarily reflecting growth in Life Sciences and Personal Care, more than offset by lower Specialty Additives and Intermediates earnings Cash flows provided by operating activities of $121 million; Ongoing Free Cash Flow2 of $103 million Reaffirming full‑year fiscal 2026 sales guidance of $1,835-$1,870 million and Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $385-$400 million WILMINGTON, Del., July 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Ashland Inc. (NYSE: ASH) today announced financial results1 for the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, which ended June 30, 2026, and reaffirmed its full-year fiscal 2026 sales and Adjusted EBITDA outlook. Ashland, a global additives and specialty ingredients company, holds leadership positions in high-quality, consumer-focused markets including pharmaceuticals, personal care and architectural coatings. “Ashland’s third-quarter results reflected broad-based demand and strong commercial execution across the portfolio,” said Guillermo Novo, chair and chief executive officer, Ashland. “Sales increased seven percent year-over-year, with growth achieved across all business units and regions. Our teams continued to successfully recover higher raw material costs through pricing actions, preserving margins while maintaining strong customer relationships. Life Sciences delivered double-digit sales gains, benefiting from broad demand across pharma and continued progress from our globalize and innovate strategies. Personal Care generated another quarter of strong performance, led by momentum in biofunctional actives, high-single-digit growth in skin care, and favorable contributions from hair care and microbial protection. Specialty Additives benefited from continued growth in coatings and performance specialties driven by share gains and strong commercial momentum. In Intermediates, merchant sales increased, reflecting improving NMP demand for battery-related applications.” Novo continued, “Our third quarter results reflected continued progress on the initiatives that are strengthening our operations and positioning the company for improved profitability over time. Plant operations improved during the quarter and profitability increased sequentially, and we recognize there is still work to do and expect continued progress as we advance our operational priorities and investments to improve reliability and throughput across the network.” “Our globalize and innovate strategies continued to exceed our targets, driven by strong customer engagement, innovation execution and momentum across our differentiated portfolio,” Novo said. “We also generated healthy cash flow in the quarter, supported by disciplined inventory management. Importantly, we ended the quarter with net leverage of 2.4x, returning to our long-term target range and further strengthening our financial flexibility. As operational performance continues to improve and production increasingly aligns with demand, we expect greater flexibility across the network and an improving profitability profile. We are also expanding the reach of our technology platforms, creating new opportunities to deliver differentiated solutions, deepen customer engagement and support long-term value creation. While the macroeconomic environment remains uncertain, we remain focused on the factors within our control, including commercial execution, operating performance, cash generation and productivity.” Third-quarter sales were $497 million, up seven percent from $463 million in the prior-year quarter. Sales volumes increased across all business units. Pricing increased by approximately one percent led by strength in Specialty Additives and Life Sciences. Foreign currency movements contributed a favorable $3 million, or one percent, to sales. Net income was $16 million, up from a loss of $742 million in the prior year. Income from continuing operations was $41 million, or $0.89 per diluted share, compared to a loss of ($15.70) last year. Adjusted Income from Continuing Operations Excluding Intangibles Amortization Expense was $47 million, down from $48 million, or $1.02 per diluted share versus $1.04 in the prior year. Adjusted Operating Income was $63 million, down from $65 million last year. Adjusted EBITDA was $109 million, representing a 21.9 percent margin, down four percent from $113 million in the prior-year quarter, as favorable volumes and pricing actions were more than offset by the lingering impact of lower production rates experienced earlier in the fiscal year, inflationary cost pressures, and the normalization of incentive compensation from a low prior-year base. Foreign currency movements contributed a favorable $1 million to Adjusted EBITDA. Average diluted shares outstanding were 46 million in the third quarter, flat versus 46 million in the prior-year quarter. Cash flows provided by operating activities were $121 million, up from $114 million in the prior-year quarter, driven primarily by working capital improvements. Ongoing Free Cash Flow totaled $103 million versus $108 million in the prior‑year quarter as ongoing free cash flow conversion rates remained above 90% in both periods. Reportable Segment Performance To aid in the understanding of Ashland’s ongoing business performance, the results of Ashland reportable segments are described below on an adjusted basis. In addition, EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA are reconciled to operating income in Table 4. Free Cash Flow, Ongoing Free Cash Flow and Adjusted Operating Income are reconciled in Table 6 and Adjusted Income from Continuing Operations, Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share and Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share Excluding Intangible Amortization Expense are reconciled in Table 7 of this news release. These adjusted results are considered non-GAAP financial measures. For a full description of the non-GAAP financial measures used, see the “Use of Non-GAAP Measures” section that further describes these adjustments below. Life Sciences Sales for the Life Sciences segment totaled $180 million in the third quarter, an increase of 11 percent compared to the prior-year quarter. Performance was driven by higher sales volumes, led by broad-based pharma demand across all major regions and product categories, continued strength in high-purity excipients and injectables, and customer order timing during the quarter. Pharma achieved double-digit sales growth, representing its fifth consecutive quarter of year-over-year volume gains, while Ashland's innovate strategy continued to support momentum in differentiated cellulose grades, injectables and low-nitrite products. Prices increased year-over-year following previously announced pricing actions, and foreign currency movements contributed a favorable impact of approximately $1 million to segment sales. Adjusted Operating Income for the quarter was $45 million, up from $40 million in the prior‑year quarter. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $60 million, representing a 33 percent margin and an 11 percent increase versus $54 million last year. The year‑over‑year increase was driven primarily by higher volumes and favorable pricing and product mix, partially offset by higher SARD. Foreign currency movements had a negligible impact on Adjusted EBITDA in the quarter. Life Sciences continues to benefit from resilient pharma demand, broad-based volume growth, and strong commercial execution, supported by ongoing momentum across its globalize and innovate strategies. Personal Care Personal Care sales in the third quarter were $155 million, an increase of five percent compared to $147 million in the prior-year quarter. Performance was driven by strong volume growth across end markets and regions, including high-single-digit growth in skin care, mid-single-digit growth in hair care and low-single-digit growth in oral and home care. Care Ingredients delivered solid gains, biofunctional actives delivered strong double-digit growth and microbial protection delivered favorable growth supported by double-digit volume gains. Performance was led by the Americas and China and supported by continued progress across Ashland's globalize and innovate strategies. Pricing improved sequentially during the quarter, while foreign currency movements contributed approximately $1 million to segment sales. Adjusted Operating Income was $30 million, up from $26 million in the prior‑year period. Adjusted EBITDA was $45 million, compared to $41 million in the prior-year quarter, representing a margin of 29 percent. Improved profitability was driven primarily by higher sales volumes and favorable product mix, partially offset by lower pricing. Personal Care delivered strong margins while continuing to advance targeted commercial and innovation initiatives across the portfolio. Specialty Additives Specialty Additives sales were $136 million in the third quarter; an increase of four percent compared to the prior-year quarter. Performance was driven by favorable pricing and mix, as continued growth in Coatings and Performance Specialties reflected strong commercial execution and share gains. These strengths more than offset the expected weakness in Construction and Energy and Resources, where market conditions remained challenged reflecting continuous softness in demand and deliberate portfolio management actions. Regionally, most markets improved compared with the prior year driven by strong execution from the commercial team. Foreign currency movements provided a favorable impact of approximately $1 million to segment sales. Adjusted Operating Income was $5 million, compared to income of $9 million in the prior-year quarter, and Adjusted EBITDA was $20 million, down from $26 million in the prior-year quarter. Results were generally in line with expectations and continued to reflect the carryover effects of the operational challenges and lower production rates discussed earlier in the fiscal year, which contributed to higher operating costs during the quarter. These impacts were partially offset by favorable pricing and product mix. Foreign currency had a negligible impact on Adjusted EBITDA during the quarter. Intermediates Intermediates sales totaled $37 million in the third quarter; an increase of twelve percent compared to $33 million in the prior-year quarter. This included $26 million in merchant sales, compared to $23 million in the prior year, and $11 million in captive butanediol (BDO) sales, up $1 million year-over-year. Captive BDO sales are recognized at market‑based pricing. Merchant sales improved, driven by higher N‑Methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) demand from North American EV battery and energy-storage customers. Foreign currency movements had a negligible impact on sales in the quarter. Adjusted Operating Income was $3 million, compared to income of $4 million in the prior-year quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $4 million, down from $7 million in the prior-year quarter. The year-over-year decline primarily reflected lower advanced manufacturing tax credit benefits compared to the prior-year quarter, while underlying operating performance remained broadly stable. Foreign currency had a negligible impact on Adjusted EBITDA during the quarter. Unallocated & Other Unallocated and other expense was $37 million compared to $49 million in the prior-year quarter. The year-over-year improvement primarily reflected favorable corporate items including lower environmental expenses and the benefit of tax credits, partially offset by higher compensation-related expenses. Adjusted unallocated and other expense EBITDA was $20 million compared to $15 million in the prior-year quarter. Financial Outlook Ashland is reaffirming its full year fiscal 2026 sales guidance of $1,835 to $1,870 million and its Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $385 to $400 million. Ashland is also revising its adjusted EPS outlook to low-to-mid-single digit growth from mid-to-high-single digit growth, reflecting a higher tax rate associated with unfavorable discrete items. The outlook reflects continued growth across the portfolio, ongoing momentum in higher value applications, increasing realization of recent pricing actions and strong cash generation. Despite a mixed macroeconomic backdrop, Ashland’s core Life Sciences and Personal Care end markets continue to demonstrate resilient demand, supported by stable fundamentals, continued innovation adoption from customers and strong commercial execution. Specialty Additives trends continue to improve, driven by share gains in coatings and performance specialties. Ashland continues to benefit from growth in differentiated, higher value applications, including biofunctional actives, microbial protection, injectables and tablet coatings. Recent pricing actions are contributing to results and are expected to provide greater benefit in the fourth quarter as realization increases. Raw material and freight costs are expected to remain elevated amid geopolitical supply pressures, although Ashland expects pricing actions to offset these impacts over time. Updated guidance Sales: $1,835 to $1,870 million (no change) Adjusted EBITDA: $385 million to $400 million (no change) Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share Excluding Intangibles Amortization: low-to-mid single-digit growth Ongoing Free Cash Flow Conversion: greater than 50 percent of Adjusted EBITDA with capital expenditures of approximately $~90 million “As we look ahead, our full year expectations reflect the underlying strength of our portfolio and the momentum we are seeing across the business,” concluded Guillermo Novo, chair and chief executive officer, Ashland. “Our globalize and innovate strategies continue to exceed expectations, demand remains resilient in our core franchise, and our teams are executing well against our innovative Technology Platforms and other priorities that support long term value creation. We expect continued sequential improvement in the fourth quarter as operational performance steadily improves. Combined with strong cash generation and disciplined execution, these actions position Ashland to carry improving earnings momentum into fiscal 2027.“ Conference Call Webcast The company’s live webcast with securities analysts will include an executive summary and detailed remarks. Use of Non-GAAP Measures Ashland believes that by removing the impact of depreciation and amortization and excluding certain non-cash charges, amounts spent on interest and taxes, and certain other charges that are highly variable from year to year, EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, EBITDA Margin and Adjusted EBITDA Margin provide Ashland’s investors with performance measures that reflect the impact to operations from trends in changes in sales, margin and operating expenses, providing a perspective not immediately apparent from net income, operating income, net income margin, and operating income margin. The adjustments Ashland makes to derive the non-GAAP measures of EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, EBITDA Margin and Adjusted EBITDA Margin exclude items which may cause short-term fluctuations in net income and operating income and which Ashland does not consider to be the fundamental attributes or primary drivers of its business. EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, EBITDA Margin, and Adjusted EBITDA Margin provide disclosure on the same basis as that used by Ashland’s management to evaluate financial performance on a consolidated and reportable segment basis and provide consistency in our financial reporting, facilitate internal and external comparisons of Ashland’s historical operating performance and its business units, and provide continuity to investors for comparability purposes. EBITDA Margin and Adjusted EBITDA Margin are defined as EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA divided by sales for the corresponding period. Key items, which are set forth on Table 7 of this release, are defined as financial effects from significant transactions that, either by their nature or amount, have caused short-term fluctuations in net income and/or operating income which Ashland does not consider to reflect Ashland’s underlying business performance and trends most accurately. Further, Ashland believes that providing supplemental information that excludes the financial effects of these items in the financial results will enhance the investor’s ability to compare financial performance between reporting periods. Tax-specific key items, which are set forth on Table 7 of this release, are defined as financial transactions, tax law changes or other matters that fall within the definition of key items as described above. These items relate solely to tax matters and would only be recorded within the income tax caption of the Statement of Consolidated Income. As with all key items, due to their nature, Ashland does not consider the financial effects of these tax-specific key items on net income to be the most accurate reflection of Ashland’s underlying business performance and trends. The Free Cash Flow metrics enable Ashland to provide a better indication of the ongoing cash being generated that is ultimately available for both debt and equity holders as well as other investment opportunities. Unlike cash flow provided by operating activities, Free Cash Flow and Ongoing Free Cash Flow include the impact of capital expenditures from continuing operations and other significant items impacting Free Cash Flow, providing a more complete picture of current and future cash generation. Free Cash Flow, Ongoing Free Cash Flow, and Ongoing Free Cash Flow Conversion are non-GAAP liquidity measures that Ashland believes provide useful information to management and investors about Ashland’s ability to convert Adjusted EBITDA to ongoing Free Cash Flow. These liquidity measures are used regularly by Ashland’s stakeholders and industry peers to measure the efficiency at providing cash from regular business activity. Free Cash Flow, Ongoing Free Cash Flow, and Free Cash Flow Conversion have certain limitations, including that they do not reflect adjustments for certain non-discretionary cash flows such as mandatory debt repayments. The amount of mandatory versus discretionary expenditures can vary significantly between periods. Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share is a performance measure used by Ashland and is defined by Ashland as earnings (loss) from continuing operations, adjusted for identified key items and divided by the number of outstanding diluted shares of common stock. Ashland believes this measure provides investors additional insights into operational performance by providing earnings and diluted earnings per share metrics that exclude the effect of the identified key items and tax specific key items. The Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share Excluding Intangibles Amortization Expense metric enables Ashland to demonstrate the impact of non-cash intangibles amortization expense on earnings per share, in addition to key items previously mentioned. Ashland’s management believes this presentation is helpful to illustrate how previous acquisitions impact applicable period results. Ashland does not quantitatively reconcile our guidance ranges for our non-GAAP measures to their most comparable GAAP measures in the Financial Outlook section of this news release. The guidance ranges for GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures reflect Ashland’s assessment of potential sources of variability in financial results and are informed by evaluation of multiple scenarios, many of which have interactive effects across several financial statement line items. Providing guidance for individual reconciling items between our non-GAAP financial measures and the comparable GAAP measures would imply a degree of precision and certainty in those reconciling items that is not a consistent reflection of our scenario-based process to prepare our guidance ranges. To the extent that a material change affecting the individual reconciling items between the company’s forward-looking non-GAAP and comparable GAAP financial measures is anticipated, the company has provided qualitative commentary in the Financial Outlook section of this news release for your consideration. However, as the impact of such factors cannot be predicted with a reasonable degree of certainty or precision, a quantitative reconciliation is not available without unreasonable effort. title: The Contact Centers That Learn Faster Will Win Faster
summary: The future of customer service belongs to organizations that learn faster. Discover how conversation intelligence, AI, and continuous feedback help contact centers turn every customer interaction into a competitive advantage.
body_text: Every contact center is generating valuable information. Every phone call, chat, email, and customer interaction contains insights about what customers want, where processes break down, and how employees succeed. The challenge isn't collecting more conversations. It's making sure the organization actually learns from them. As AI becomes more accessible and conversation intelligence becomes more common, the organizations that outperform their competitors won't necessarily be the ones with the newest technology. They'll be the ones that learn, adapt, and improve the fastest. Data Doesn't Create Competitive Advantage For years, organizations have invested heavily in collecting more information. More dashboards. More reports. More KPIs. More transcripts. But information alone doesn't improve customer experience. An organization doesn't become better simply because it has access to more data. It becomes better when that information leads to better decisions, stronger coaching, and smarter operational changes. The real value isn't in collecting conversations. It's in learning from them. Every Conversation Is Feedback Customer conversations are one of the richest sources of operational intelligence in any business. Every day, customers reveal where policies create confusion, which products generate frustration, what competitors are doing differently, and which explanations build trust. At the same time, agents are constantly discovering better ways to communicate, solve problems, and navigate difficult situations. Unfortunately, much of that learning never spreads beyond the individual interaction. The conversation ends, the transcript is stored, and the insight quietly disappears. Imagine if every successful de-escalation technique, every recurring customer complaint, and every coaching opportunity immediately became part of how the organization operated going forward. That's what learning organizations strive to achieve. The Best Organizations Build Learning Loops High-performing contact centers don't treat conversations as isolated events. They treat every interaction as an opportunity to improve the business. Customer insights help refine processes. QA findings improve coaching. Agent feedback strengthens knowledge bases. Operational trends influence training. AI systems become more effective because they're continuously informed by real customer interactions. Instead of asking, "What happened on this call?" they begin asking, "What should this conversation teach us?" That subtle shift changes the role of the contact center. It becomes more than a support organization. It becomes one of the company's most valuable learning engines. Speed Matters More Than Perfection One of the biggest mistakes organizations make is waiting too long to act on what they learn. A recurring customer issue gets discussed during next month's operations meeting. A coaching opportunity waits until the next training session. A process improvement sits in someone's notebook for weeks while customers continue experiencing the same friction. The organizations that improve fastest create short feedback loops. They identify patterns quickly, validate insights quickly, and make changes while those insights are still fresh. Small improvements made every week often create a much larger competitive advantage than massive initiatives launched once a year. Technology Should Make Improvement Easier AI is making it possible to learn from conversations at a scale that simply wasn't possible a few years ago. Conversation intelligence can surface recurring patterns across thousands of interactions. Automated QA identifies coaching opportunities consistently instead of relying on small samples. High-quality transcription provides an accurate foundation for analysis, while intuitive tools make it easier for managers to turn insights into action. The technology itself isn't the competitive advantage. The competitive advantage is how quickly an organization can learn from what the technology uncovers. The Bottom Line Over the next few years, most contact centers will have access to similar AI capabilities. What will separate great organizations from average ones won't be who purchased AI first. It will be who learned the fastest. Every customer conversation has the potential to improve your people, your processes, your knowledge, and your customer experience. The organizations that recognize that won't just keep up with change. They'll be the ones leading it.

title: Wedding Speech Examples for Every Role: Bride, Groom, Best Man, Maid of Honor & More

body_text: Last Updated on July 27, 2026 by Joy Editors Quick Answer A great wedding speech has five parts: introduce yourself, share one specific story, connect it to the couple’s relationship, offer genuine wishes for their future, and close with a toast. Aim for 300-600 words (2-4 minutes). The traditional speaking order is father of the bride, best man, maid of honor, then the couple. Below you will find fill-in-the-blank templates, full examples for every role, a writing timeline, toast lines, and a clear list of what not to say. Wedding speeches are one of the most memorable parts of any reception, and one of the most nerve-wracking to write. Whether you are the best man scrambling for the right words, the maid of honor trying to balance funny and heartfelt, or the bride or groom wanting to thank the people who made the day possible, this guide has you covered. Below you will find the speaking order, fill-in-the-blank templates, full speech examples for every role, a week-by-week writing timeline, quotable toast lines, and practical tips for delivering your words with confidence. Wedding Speech Order: Who Speaks and When The speaking order matters more than most people expect. It controls the emotional arc of the evening: welcome, then warmth, then humor, then gratitude. Get it wrong and the room peaks too early, or the funny speech lands right after the tearful one and feels jarring. Here is the traditional order, which still works at the majority of weddings: Order Speaker Length Purpose 1 Father of the bride (or both parents of the bride) 3-5 min Welcomes guests, sets the emotional tone, welcomes the new partner into the family 2 Father of the groom or parents of the groom 2-4 min Thanks the hosts, welcomes the other family, offers a blessing 3 Best man 3-5 min Brings the humor, tells one great story, toasts the couple 4 Maid of honor 3-5 min Balances humor with real feeling, speaks to the bride directly 5 Groom (or the couple together) 2-4 min Thanks everyone: families, wedding party, guests who traveled 6 Bride 2-4 min Closes the block, speaks to her partner, raises the final toast Most modern weddings adjust this. Blended families, two brides, two grooms, absent parents, and couples who simply do not want six speeches all call for a different shape. These variations are common and completely acceptable: Situation Suggested Order You want to keep it short (3 speeches total) Parent of the bride, best man or maid of honor (pick one), then the couple together Two brides or two grooms One parent from each family, then each member of the wedding party, then each partner. Alternate families so neither goes first twice. Blended or step-families Group parents and step-parents into one joint welcome, or split across the rehearsal dinner and reception so nobody is left out A parent has passed away Have a sibling, aunt, uncle, or family friend speak in that slot, or add a brief moment of remembrance in the couple’s speech Large wedding party who all want to speak Move extra speeches to the rehearsal dinner or welcome party. Cap the reception at four. Very casual or micro wedding Open-mic style after dinner, with one designated person to start and close it Where speeches sit in the evening: The safest slot is after the main course and before dessert. Guests have eaten, nobody is light-headed, and the bar has not been open so long that the room stops listening. Avoid scheduling speeches during cocktail hour (people are standing and distracted) or after dancing has started (you will never get the energy back). How Many Speeches Is Too Many Four is the sweet spot. Five is fine. Six is the ceiling. Beyond that, guests lose attention regardless of how good the individual speeches are. The practical constraint is total time, not the number of speakers. Budget 20 to 25 minutes for the entire speech block, including the pauses while people find the microphone and get settled. Two speakers at eight minutes each is worse than five speakers at four minutes each. Number of Speeches Total Block Time Works Well For 2-3 10-15 min Micro weddings, courthouse celebrations, couples who want dinner to move quickly 4-5 18-25 min Most weddings. Enough voices to feel full without dragging. 6 25-30 min Large weddings with two full families to acknowledge. Split into two blocks if possible. 7+ 30+ min Not recommended at a reception. Move the overflow to the rehearsal dinner. Who Introduces Each Speaker Somebody has to say “and now we will hear from the best man.” Do not leave this to chance, because the alternative is an awkward silence while five people look at each other. A professional MC or the band leader. Cleanest option. Give them the running order in writing, with correct name pronunciations. The DJ. Works well and costs nothing extra. Confirm they are comfortable doing it, since not all DJs are. One member of the wedding party. A good choice for smaller weddings. Ask someone who is not also giving a long speech. A parent. Traditional at some weddings: the father of the bride opens the block and hands off to each speaker. Whoever does it should hold a printed list. Phones die, screens dim, and reading the order off a text message in a dark room does not work. If you are printing wedding programs , including the speech order gives guests a heads-up and gently signals to speakers that the schedule is real. Speakers need to know when they are on well before the day. Publishing a schedule of events that lists the reception timeline means nobody is surprised, and the wedding party can plan around it. For the broader picture of how the speech block fits into the evening, see this guide to building a reception timeline , and these practical tips for setting up speeches . The Anatomy of a Great Wedding Speech Every memorable wedding speech, regardless of who is giving it, follows a similar structure. Use this as your framework: Section What to Include Approximate Length Opening Who you are, your relationship to the couple 30-60 seconds Story One specific, vivid memory that shows who they are 60-90 seconds Connection How that story reflects the couple’s relationship or values 30-45 seconds Wishes Genuine hopes for their future together 30-45 seconds Toast Short, punchy, glass-raising close 15-20 seconds The 50/30/20 Rule: Spend 50% of your speech on the person you know best, 30% on the couple together, and 20% on the guests and occasion. This keeps the speech personal without ignoring the new partner or the celebration itself. Wedding Speech Templates You Can Fill In If you are staring at a blank page, start here. How to use a template without sounding like one: Fill it in, then delete the first sentence of every paragraph and see if the speech still works. It usually does, and it is tighter. Templates give you structure, but the specific details are what make the room go quiet. Best Man Speech Examples The best man speech is expected to be funny, warm, and brief. One good story beats three mediocre ones. The job is not to be the funniest person in the room: it is to make the groom look good and make the couple feel celebrated. Humor is the delivery mechanism, not the point. At a Glance Best Man Typical length 3-5 minutes (400-600 words) Position in the order Usually third, after the parents Tone Funny opening, sincere finish. Land the plane on warmth. Must include Your name, how you know the groom, one story, a direct line to the partner, a clear toast Avoid Ex-partners, bachelor party details, inside jokes, anything you would not say in front of his grandmother Common mistake Roasting for four minutes and never saying anything kind Example 1: Classic Best Man Good evening, everyone. For those I have not met, I am [Name], and I have had the privilege of being [Groom’s] best friend for the past twelve years. In that time, I have watched him make a lot of decisions: some excellent, some I will not mention tonight. Marrying [Partner’s Name] is, without question, the best one he has ever made. I knew [Partner’s Name] was different the first time [Groom] talked about them. He did not just say “I met someone.” He said “I think this is the person.” That is not something he says lightly. And watching them together these past few years, I can tell you: he was right. [Groom], you are one of the most loyal, generous people I know. [Partner’s Name], you make him even better. That is the highest compliment I can give anyone. Please raise your glasses. To [Groom] and [Partner’s Name]: may your love be modern enough to survive the times, and old-fashioned enough to last forever. Cheers. Example 2: Funny Best Man Good evening. I am [Name], and I have been asked to keep this speech under five minutes. I have been asked to keep a lot of things under five minutes over the years, and I have never once succeeded. Tonight, I will try. I have known [Groom] since we were both terrible at most things. He has improved significantly. [Partner’s Name] deserves a large share of the credit for that. I have watched [Groom] fall in love before. It never looked like this. This looks like the real thing: the kind where you actually listen when the other person is talking, where you remember their coffee order, where you become a slightly better version of yourself just by being around them. [Partner’s Name], thank you for making him that person. And [Groom], thank you for finally giving me a reason to buy a suit. To the couple: may your arguments be short, your adventures be long, and your Wi-Fi always be strong. Cheers. Example 3: Best Man Who Is Also the Brother Good evening. I am [Name], and I am [Groom’s] younger brother, which means I have spent my entire life either following him around or arguing with him. Usually both in the same afternoon. Here is what I know about my brother that most of you do not. When our family went through a hard year, he was nineteen, and he drove four hours every other weekend to be home. Nobody asked him to. He never mentioned it. He just kept showing up. That is the thing about [Groom]. He shows up. Quietly, without needing credit for it. [Partner’s Name], you are getting a person who will show up for you for the rest of your life. I know that because I have watched him do it. And I want to say thank you, because in the last few years I have watched him become lighter, funnier, and more himself than I have ever seen him. Please raise your glasses. To my brother and [Partner’s Name]. Cheers. Maid of Honor Speech Examples The maid of honor speech should balance humor with genuine emotion. You know the bride better than almost anyone. Let that show. One personal story, a moment of real feeling, and a warm toast lands better than a list of compliments. At a Glance Maid of Honor Typical length 3-5 minutes (400-600 words) Position in the order Usually fourth, right after the best man Tone Warm and personal, with humor woven through rather than front-loaded Must include How you met, one story that shows her character, a direct line to her partner, a toast Avoid Dating history, anything about her family that is not yours to share, lists of adjectives Common mistake Talking only about the bride and forgetting the partner exists Example 1: Classic Maid of Honor Hi, everyone. I am [Name], and I have been [Bride’s] best friend since we were both [age] and had very questionable taste in everything. Some things have changed. Most things have not. [Bride] is one of the most thoughtful people I have ever known. She remembers birthdays, she shows up when things are hard, and she gives advice that is actually useful. I have always admired that about her. When she told me about [Partner’s Name], I noticed something different. She was not just happy: she was calm. Like she had found something she had been looking for without quite knowing she was looking. That is a rare thing. [Partner’s Name], you make my best friend feel like the best version of herself. That is everything I could have asked for. Please raise your glasses, to [Bride] and [Partner’s Name]. May every day together feel as good as today. Cheers. Example 2: Funny Maid of Honor Good evening, everyone. I am [Name], [Bride’s] maid of honor and, more importantly, the person who has heard every version of this love story since the very beginning. I was there for the first text she sent me after their first date. I will not read it aloud, but I will say it involved a lot of capital letters and at least three exclamation points per sentence. That is not her normal style. [Bride], you have always known exactly who you are and what you want. Watching you find someone who matches that energy, who makes you laugh as hard as you make everyone else laugh, has been one of the great joys of my life. [Partner’s Name], welcome to the family. Fair warning: we are a lot. You are handling it beautifully. To the couple: may your love story always be worth reading. Cheers. Example 3: Maid of Honor Who Is Also the Sister Hi, everyone. I am [Name], and I am [Bride’s] sister. I have known her longer than anyone in this room, including our parents, who technically arrived first but were not paying as close attention. When we were kids, [Bride] used to organize everything. Our toys, our schedules, our arguments. She once made a written agreement about whose turn it was to sit in the front seat. She was seven. It was laminated. I used to find that annoying. Now I understand it differently. She takes care of the people she loves by making sure nothing falls through the cracks. That is not control. That is love with a spreadsheet. [Partner’s Name], you are marrying someone who will remember every important date, notice when you are quiet, and handle the hard things before you know they are happening. Do not take that for granted, and I do not think you will, because I have watched how you look at her. To my sister and [Partner’s Name]. Cheers. Father of the Bride Speech Examples The father of the bride speech is traditionally the first of the evening. It sets the emotional tone. Keep it warm, personal, and brief. Welcome the new partner into the family, thank the guests, and give the couple your blessing. At a Glance Father of the Bride Typical length 3-5 minutes (400-600 words) Position in the order First. You open the block and set the tone. Tone Warm, proud, a little emotional. Humor is welcome but not required. Must include A welcome to all guests, one memory of your daughter, an explicit welcome to her partner, a blessing Avoid Money talk, advice that sounds like instructions, jokes about “losing” a daughter Common mistake Talking about your daughter for four minutes and mentioning her partner once, at the end Example 1: Traditional Father of the Bride Good evening, everyone. For those I have not had the pleasure of meeting, I am [Name], [Bride’s] father, and the proudest person in this room tonight. I have watched [Bride] grow from someone who needed me for everything into someone who needs me for very little, and that is exactly how it is supposed to go. She is kind, she is capable, and she has always known her own mind. I cannot take full credit for that, but I will take some. [Partner’s Name], I want you to know that you are not just gaining a spouse today. You are gaining a family that will show up for you, celebrate with you, and occasionally give you unsolicited advice. We come as a package. I hope that is acceptable. To my daughter and her partner: your mother and I wish you a life full of the things that matter. Good health, real laughter, and the kind of love that gets better with time. Please raise your glasses. To [Bride] and [Partner’s Name]. Example 2: Father of the Bride, Blended Family Good evening. I am [Name], and I am lucky enough to be one of the people who helped raise [Bride]. I want to start by thanking every person in this room who had a hand in getting her here. Her mother, her stepmother, her grandparents, the teachers and friends who showed up along the way. It took a lot of people, and none of us did it alone. Here is what I remember most. [Bride] was [age] when she decided she was going to [specific childhood ambition]. Everyone told her it would be difficult. She did it anyway, and she has been doing exactly that ever since. She decides, and then she does it. [Partner’s Name], you have been part of this family for a while now, and today just makes it official on paper. You have been steady, you have been kind to her, and you have been patient with all of us. Welcome, formally. To [Bride] and [Partner’s Name]: may you keep choosing each other, on the easy days and the difficult ones. Please raise your glasses. Father of the Groom Speech Examples The father of the groom speech is shorter than the father of the bride speech and serves a slightly different purpose: thank the hosts, welcome the other family, and offer a blessing. If the bride’s family hosted, acknowledging that directly is the traditional courtesy. At a Glance Father of the Groom Typical length 2-4 minutes (250-450 words) Position in the order Second, after the father or parents of the bride Tone Gracious and appreciative. This is the thank-you speech. Must include Thanks to the hosts, a welcome to the new family, one line about your son, a blessing Avoid Repeating what the previous speaker just said, going longer than the bride’s father did Common mistake Treating it as a second best man speech Example: Father of the Groom Good evening. I am [Name], [Groom’s] father, and I will be brief, because [previous speaker] said most of it better than I could. First, thank you to [Bride’s parents] for tonight, for your generosity, and for raising a daughter we are genuinely thrilled to welcome into our family. That is not a formality. We mean it. [Groom], I have watched you work hard for everything you have. You have never asked anyone to make it easier for you. I have always admired that, even when I wished you would ask for help occasionally. [Bride’s Name], you have made him happier than I have seen him. A parent does not need much more than that. To the two of you: build something that lasts, be kind to each other on the ordinary days, and come home for dinner now and then. Please raise your glasses. Mother of the Bride and Mother of the Groom Speech Examples Mothers giving speeches used to be the exception. It is now common, and often the most affecting speech of the night. There is no separate etiquette to learn: the structure is the same as any parent speech. Speak to your child, welcome their partner explicitly, and thank the room. At a Glance Mother of the Bride or Groom Typical length 2-4 minutes (250-450 words) Position in the order Either alongside your partner in the opening slot, or as your own speech in the first two positions Tone Personal and specific. Parent speeches earn the right to be sentimental. I am [Name], and I am [Bride’s] mother. Thank you for being here. Some of you traveled a long way, and I know what that costs in time and effort. It means a great deal to us that you came. I was wrong about that. What she actually needed was to understand things by explaining them, and she still does it, and it is one of my favorite things about her. I am [Name], [Groom’s] mother, and I have been looking forward to this for a very long time. Somewhere along the way you turned all of that into a person people rely on, and I am prouder of that than of anything on your resume. [Bride’s Name], you brought out a side of him I had not seen since he was very young. He is lighter with you. He laughs more. Thank you for that, sincerely. Groom Speech Examples The groom’s speech is a thank-you speech with one personal moment at the end. Thank the hosts, the families, the wedding party, and the guests who traveled, then say something real to your partner. Two to four minutes is plenty. At a Glance Groom Typical length 2-4 minutes (250-450 words) Position in the order Near the end, before or alongside the bride Tone Grateful, warm, direct. Nerves are fine and the room is on your side. Must include Thanks to both families, thanks to the wedding party, thanks to travelers, one line to your partner Avoid Trying to be funnier than the best man, thanking a long list by name and forgetting someone Common mistake Making it entirely logistics and gratitude with nothing personal in it Example 1: Groom, Simple and Sincere I will be honest: I have rewritten this speech four times. Every version sounded either too formal or too much like a toast at a work event. So I am going to keep it simple. Thank you. To our families, who gave us everything. To our friends, who showed up. To the people who traveled far to be here: we do not take that lightly. [Partner’s Name], I have been trying to figure out how to say what I want to say, and I keep coming back to this: you make ordinary days feel significant. That is not a small thing. That is everything. I am the luckiest person in this room. Please raise your glasses. To my partner, my best friend, and the person I get to spend my life with. Cheers. Example 2: Groom, With a Story Good evening, everyone, and thank you for being here. I want to thank both of our families, our wedding party for carrying us through the last year, and everyone who got on a plane to be in this room. I want to tell you about a Tuesday. Not a big moment, not the proposal. A Tuesday about two years ago, when I had a bad day and came home and did not want to talk about it. [Partner’s Name] did not ask me any questions. She made dinner, put on something terrible on television, and sat next to me for three hours. That was the day I knew. Not because of anything she said, but because of how easy it was to be a mess in front of her. [Partner’s Name], I am not going to promise you a perfect life. I am going to promise you that when it is not perfect, I will be sitting next to you. Please raise your glasses. To my wife. Cheers. Bride Speech Examples Brides speak at most weddings now, either alongside their partner or on their own. The structure mirrors the groom’s speech: gratitude first, then one genuine thing said out loud to the person you married. At a Glance Bride Typical length 2-4 minutes (250-450 words) Position in the order Last, closing the block with the final toast Tone Whatever is actually true for you. Funny, tender, or plainspoken all work. Must include Thanks to families and guests, acknowledgment of your wedding party, one line to your partner Avoid Apologizing for being emotional, reading a long thank-you list, running past four minutes Common mistake Assuming you do not need to prepare because you will “just speak from the heart” Example 1: Bride, Gratitude First I want to start by saying thank you. To everyone in this room for traveling, for celebrating with us, and for making today feel like the most loved we have ever been. To our wedding party: you have been extraordinary. You showed up for every moment, every errand, every late-night panic. We see you and we are so grateful. To our parents: everything good about us started with you. Thank you for teaching us what love looks like in practice, not just in words, but in the daily choices you made for your families. And to [Partner’s Name]: I did not know it was possible to feel this sure about anything. You are my favorite person to talk to, to travel with, to disagree with, and to come home to. [Partner’s Name], I used to think the goal was to find someone who agreed with me. It turns out the goal was to find someone I trust when we disagree. That is you, and I did not know to look for it. Please raise your glasses. To all of you, to this ridiculous and wonderful day, and to my husband. Cheers. Short Wedding Speech Examples (Under 2 Minutes) Not every speech needs to be long. A short, well-crafted toast can be more memorable than a rambling five-minute speech. These work for anyone giving a brief toast at the rehearsal dinner, the reception, or a smaller celebration. You are exactly what we hoped for. To both of you: cheers. That says something about you, and it says something about the life you are building. To [Name] and [Partner’s Name]: sleep well, and we will see you tomorrow. Cheers. Wedding Speech Timeline: When to Write, Practice, and Deliver Most bad wedding speeches are not written badly. They are written late. The speech that gets drafted the night before is almost always the one that runs long, wanders, and leans on generic praise because there was no time to find the real story. Here is a schedule that works. It assumes about three hours of total effort, spread out so your brain has time to do the useful background work between sessions. When What to Do Time Needed 8 weeks out Confirm you are speaking, how long you have, and where you sit in the order. Ask the couple if anything is off-limits. 10 minutes 6 weeks out Collect raw material. Open a note on your phone and add memories as they occur to you. Do not write yet, just gather. Ongoing, 5 minutes at a time 4 weeks out Pick one story. Write a messy first draft in one sitting without editing. Aim for 600-800 words and expect to cut. 45 minutes 3 weeks out Cut to 400-600 words. Delete anything that needs explaining. Read it aloud once and time it. 30 minutes 2 weeks out Send it to one trusted person, ideally someone who knows the couple. Ask specifically: is anything here unclear, unkind, or too long? 15 minutes 1 week out Final version. Print two copies on note cards in large type. Memorize your first line and your last line. 30 minutes 3 days out Practice out loud, standing, three times. Time each run. If it is over your limit, cut, do not speed up. 20 minutes Day before One run-through. Put a printed copy in the pocket of whatever you are wearing tomorrow. Do not rewrite tonight. 10 minutes Wedding day Read it once quietly in the morning. Then leave it alone until you are called up. 5 minutes If you have one week, not eight: Do the 4-week step tonight (messy draft, one story, no editing), the 3-week cut tomorrow, and practice out loud three times over the remaining days. The single non-negotiable step is reading it out loud standing up. Skipping that is what causes speeches to run double their intended length. Wedding Day Timing: What Happens When Knowing the shape of the evening keeps you calm. Here is the typical sequence at a reception with a seated dinner: Approximate Time What Is Happening What Speakers Should Do Cocktail hour Guests arrive, drinks are served Limit yourself to one drink. Locate the microphone and the person running the order. Guests seated Couple enters, first course begins Confirm the running order has not changed. It often has. After the main course Plates cleared, glasses topped up This is usually when the speech block starts. Have your cards in hand. Speech block (20-25 min) Speakers go in order Stand where the couple can see you. Do not start until the room is quiet. Dessert and cake Energy shifts, guests start moving Speeches are over. Do not add one now. Dancing Music takes over Hand your printed copy to someone who can keep it. The couple often wants it later. How to Write Your Own Wedding Speech: Step by Step Start with one story. Do not try to summarize the entire relationship. Pick one specific memory that captures who they are: a moment, a conversation, a decision they made that told you everything. Write the way you talk. Read your draft aloud. If it sounds like an essay, rewrite it. The best speeches sound like a conversation. Keep it to 300-600 words. At a comfortable speaking pace (about 130-150 words per minute), that is 2-4 minutes. Time yourself. Address both partners by name. Even if you only know one of them well, acknowledge the other directly. It matters. Practice out loud at least three times. Not in your head, out loud, standing up, at speaking pace. You will catch awkward phrases you would miss on paper. End with a clear toast line. “Please raise your glasses” is your signal. Have your closing line memorized so you can deliver it with confidence. Opening Lines That Work The first 15 seconds set the tone for everything that follows. Here are opening lines that work for different roles and styles: “I have known [Name] for [X] years, and in that time I have learned three things about them.” (Best man or maid of honor: sets up a list structure) “When [Name] asked me to speak today, I said yes immediately. Then I spent three weeks regretting it.” (Funny: relatable and self-aware) “There are people in your life who make you better just by being in it. [Name] is one of those people.” (Warm: works for any role) “I am [Name]’s [role], which means I have a front-row seat to one of the best love stories I know.” (Parent: sets up a narrative) “I have been trying to figure out what to say tonight, and I keep coming back to one word: grateful.” (Bride or groom: honest and direct) “I am going to tell you about a Tuesday.” (Any role: an unexpected opener that earns attention immediately) “There are two versions of this speech. The one I wrote, and the one I would have given if [Name] were not sitting eight feet away.” (Funny: works if you follow it with something genuinely kind) Wedding Speech Quotes and Toast Lines These are original lines written to be borrowed. Use them as a closing toast, an opening hook, or the sentence that carries the emotional weight of your speech. Change the wording so it sounds like you, and never use more than one per speech: a stack of quotable lines reads as a greeting card rather than a person speaking. Heartfelt “Love is not the part where you find each other. It is the ten thousand ordinary days you choose each other afterward.” “The best marriages are not built on grand gestures. They are built on being the first person the other one wants to tell.” “You did not complete each other. You were both already whole. You just decided the view was better side by side.” “There is a particular kind of luck in finding someone who makes you feel like the most normal version of yourself. That is what I see when I look at you two.” “A good partner does not remove the difficult parts of life. They just make you feel less alone inside them.” “May you always be each other’s easiest room to walk into.” Funny “Marriage is the only contract where both parties are hoping for an unlimited extension.” “To a long marriage: may you argue about small things, agree on the big ones, and never disagree about the thermostat at the same time.” “They say you should marry your best friend. These two took it further and became genuinely insufferable about it.” “May your love last longer than your appliances, and may your appliances last a very long time.” “To the couple: may you always split the last slice, and may neither of you ever admit who wanted it more.” “I have been told a good toast should be short, sincere, and memorable. I have managed two out of three, and I will let you decide which.” Short and Classic “To love, laughter, and a very long story.” “To the two of you, and the life you are about to build.” “To a marriage as good as this party.” “To the beginning of the best part.” “To choosing each other, today and on every ordinary day after.” For Couples Who Have Been Together a Long Time “Some couples get married to begin their life together. These two got married to make it official for the paperwork.” “You have already done the hard parts. Moving, deadlines, family, a difficult year or two. Today is just the celebration you earned somewhere along the way.” “After [number] years, nobody here needed convincing. We were just waiting for the party.” For Blended Families and Second Marriages “Today is not just two people joining. It is a whole family deciding to be one thing instead of several.” “Some of the best families are the ones that were assembled on purpose.” “There is something brave about choosing this again, and something wonderful about watching you choose it so well.” Closing Toast Lines “Please raise your glasses. To [Name] and [Name], and to everyone lucky enough to be in this room.” “Everyone, on your feet. To the couple.” “Glasses up. To a long, loud, well-loved life together.” “To [Name] and [Name]. May today be the least happy day of your marriage.” What Not to Say in a Wedding Speech Speeches rarely fail because of what was missing. They fail because of one line that should have been cut. Almost every wedding speech disaster falls into one of the categories below, and every one of them is avoidable in a single editing pass. The Hard No List Do Not Say Why It Fails Say This Instead Anything about an ex-partner There is no version of this that lands. It embarrasses the couple and puts the room on edge. Talk about what changed when they met their partner, without a comparison “I am not good at speeches” Signals the audience to lower expectations before you have said anything Open directly with your name and your relationship to the couple Bachelor or bachelorette party details Grandparents, colleagues, and children are in the room “We had a very good weekend, and that is all anyone needs to know” Jokes about the marriage failing The “ball and chain” genre reads as bitter, not funny, to most of the room Humor about the couple’s quirks, not about marriage as an institution Anything about money Cost of the wedding, who paid, salaries, or the value of gifts Thank the hosts for their generosity without naming figures References to pregnancy or grandchildren You may be wrong, and even if you are right it is not your announcement Wish them a full life together and stop there Reading a list of everyone’s names Loses the room in twenty seconds and you will still forget someone Thank groups: families, wedding party, everyone who traveled Inside jokes for five people The other 145 guests sit in silence, which changes the energy of the whole speech Explain the context in one sentence, or cut the joke Comparisons between the two families Even a compliment framed as a comparison creates a loser Say something specific and warm about each family separately “I will keep this short” (then not doing it) The room starts counting. You have set a timer against yourself. Just be short. Do not announce it. Subjects to Handle Carefully, Not Avoid Some topics are not off-limits, but they need to be handled deliberately rather than improvised: A parent or loved one who has died. One sentence, placed early, delivered plainly. “I know [Name] would have loved to be here tonight.” Do not build the speech around it, and do not skip it if the family would notice the absence. Divorced or estranged parents. Acknowledge everyone in a group phrase rather than individually. Check with the couple beforehand on names and titles: guessing at how to refer to a step-parent is the most common source of hurt feelings in parent speeches. Faith and religion. Follow the couple’s lead. If the ceremony was religious, a blessing fits. If it was not, keep it universal. The couple’s difficult year. Illness, job loss, a long-distance stretch. Only include it if it is genuinely part of their story and only if you have asked. What reads as resilience to you may read as private to them. Politics, work grievances, and current events. There is no upside. Cut them. Delivery Mistakes That Undo a Good Speech Drinking to settle your nerves. One drink is calming. Three is detectable from every seat in the room. Hold off until after you have spoken. Reading from your phone. The screen dims, the lighting is wrong, and it looks like you are checking messages. Use printed note cards in large type. Going over time. A five-minute speech at four minutes is charming. At nine minutes it is a problem the couple will remember. Explaining a joke that did not land. Move on immediately. The room forgets in four seconds if you do. Adding “one more thing” after the toast. The toast is the ending. Once glasses are up, you are finished. Turning your back on the couple. Stand so they are in your eyeline. Most of the speech should be delivered to them, not to the room. The one-question edit: Read your final draft and ask, for every line, “would I be comfortable if the couple read this before the wedding?” If the answer is no anywhere, cut that line. A speech that only works as a surprise is a speech that should not be given. Make Sure Every Guest Knows When Speeches Start A great speech deserves a great audience, and that comes down to logistics. Publish the reception timeline on your wedding website so speakers know their slot and guests are seated when the block begins. Managing RSVPs and the schedule in one place also means late changes reach everyone automatically, which matters more than most couples expect on the day. For more on who speaks and what is expected of each role, see this guide to wedding party etiquette . Delivery Tips: How to Give a Great Wedding Speech Do Avoid Practice out loud at least 3 times Reading word-for-word without looking up Speak slowly: nerves make you rush Going over 5 minutes Make eye contact with the couple Staring at your notes the whole time Pause after jokes and let them land Explaining the joke if it does not land Hold the mic 1-2 inches from your lips Tapping or moving the mic around Print note cards in large type Reading from your phone screen Wait for the room to go quiet before starting Talking over conversation and clinking cutlery End with a clear, confident toast line Adding “one more thing” after the toast FAQ: Wedding Speeches What do you say for a wedding speech? A wedding speech typically includes an introduction (who you are and your relationship to the couple), a personal story or memory, warm wishes for the couple’s future, and a toast. Aim for 2-4 minutes (300-600 words). Keep it heartfelt, specific, and positive. What is the order of speeches at a wedding? The traditional order is: father of the bride, father of the groom, best man, maid of honor, groom, then bride. Most modern weddings shorten this to three or four speeches. The order matters because it controls the emotional arc of the evening: welcome first, humor in the middle, gratitude at the end. When during the reception should speeches happen? After the main course and before dessert. Guests have eaten, the room is seated and attentive, and the bar has not been open long enough for attention to fade. Avoid cocktail hour (guests are standing and distracted) and anything after dancing has started. What is the best opening line for a wedding speech? The best opening lines introduce yourself, establish your relationship to the couple, and hook the audience immediately. Try: “I have known [Name] for [X] years, and in that time I have watched them become the person standing here today.” Avoid opening with “I am not good at speeches,” which tells the room to expect less. How long should a wedding speech be? Most wedding speeches run 2-4 minutes (300-600 words at a comfortable pace). Best man and maid of honor speeches typically run 3-5 minutes. Bride and groom speeches can be shorter. Avoid going over 5 minutes, since guests’ attention fades quickly. Budget 20-25 minutes for the entire speech block. How many speeches should there be at a wedding? Four is the sweet spot and six is the ceiling. Total time matters more than the number of speakers: five four-minute speeches work better than two eight-minute ones. If more people want to speak, move the extra speeches to the rehearsal dinner or welcome party. Does the mother of the bride give a speech? Often, yes. Mothers speaking at weddings is now common, either alongside their partner in the opening slot or as a separate speech. The structure is the same as any parent speech: one real memory, an explicit welcome to the new partner, and a wish for the marriage. Keep it to 2-4 minutes. What is the 50/30/20 rule for wedding speeches? The 50/30/20 rule suggests spending 50% of your speech on the person you know best, 30% on the couple together, and 20% on the guests and occasion. It keeps the speech personal without ignoring the new partner or the celebration itself. When should I start writing my wedding speech? Start collecting memories about six weeks out and write your first draft four weeks before the wedding. That leaves time to cut it down, get one round of feedback, and practice out loud. Total effort is around three hours. Speeches written the night before are the ones that run long and rely on generic praise. Can I use quotes in a wedding speech? Yes, but use one at most, and place it where it carries weight: usually the closing toast. A speech built from borrowed lines feels like a greeting card. Adapt the wording so it sounds like something you would actually say out loud. What should you never say in a wedding speech? Never mention ex-partners, bachelor or bachelorette party details, money, pregnancy speculation, or jokes about the marriage failing. Skip inside jokes that only a handful of guests understand, and do not compare the two families. If you would not be comfortable with the couple reading a line beforehand, cut it. Who gives speeches at a wedding? Traditional wedding speeches come from the best man, maid of honor, father of the bride, and the couple themselves. Modern weddings often include the mother of the bride or groom, a sibling, or close friends. Blended families, two brides, or two grooms all call for a custom order, which is completely standard.
